nameStory: The common laburnum earned its nickname 'golden chain' from its spectacular drooping clusters of bright yellow flowers that hang like ornamental chains from the branches. The name 'golden rain' comes from the way the petals flutter down like golden droplets when they fall, creating a magical carpet beneath the tree.
description: Common laburnum is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that typically grows 15-25 feet tall with an open, graceful branching pattern. In late spring, it transforms into a stunning display of pendulous yellow flower clusters that can reach 6-10 inches long, hanging like golden waterfalls from every branch. The compound leaves have three oval leaflets, giving it a delicate, almost tropical appearance despite its European origins.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Long, drooping clusters of bright golden-yellow pea-like flowers hang from branches in late spring, each cluster 6-10 inches long with a sweet, honey-like fragrance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part compound leaves with oval leaflets that feel smooth and slightly waxy, arranged alternately on branches with a silvery-green underside

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, brown seed pods 2-3 inches long that twist when ripe, containing small dark seeds - all parts are highly poisonous

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray-brown bark when young, developing shallow furrows with age, often with a slightly greenish tinge on younger branches

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small tree or large shrub with an open, somewhat weeping form and gracefully arching branches that create an elegant silhouette

habitat: In New England, common laburnum is found primarily as an ornamental planting in parks, gardens, and residential areas, rarely naturalizing in the wild. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade, though it flowers best in sunny locations. You're most likely to encounter it around older homes and estates where it was planted for its spectacular spring display.

seasonality.spring: The main show happens in late spring (May-June) when the tree erupts in cascades of golden-yellow flower clusters that are visible from quite a distance.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, the three-part leaves provide light shade, and flat seed pods begin developing that will persist through the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn a modest yellow before dropping, and the brown seed pods become more prominent as they mature and split open.
seasonality.winter: The bare branches reveal the tree's graceful architecture, with persistent seed pods often remaining attached, and smooth gray bark becoming more noticeable.

funFact: Despite its beauty, every part of the common laburnum contains highly toxic alkaloids - the seeds were once called 'false ebony' and used to make jewelry, but this practice was abandoned when people realized how dangerous they were to handle and work with.
confusionNotes: The drooping yellow flower clusters are so distinctive that laburnum is rarely confused with other plants when in bloom, but the three-part leaves might be mistaken for those of other legumes like false indigo - remember that laburnum's flowers hang in long chains, while most similar plants have upright flower clusters.
contextualKnowledge: Though beautiful, laburnum is considered one of the most poisonous trees commonly planted as an ornamental, earning it the nickname 'golden death' in some circles - all parts contain cytisine, which can be fatal if ingested, making it a controversial choice for public plantings despite its spectacular beauty.
compareHints: Common laburnum is the only Laburnum species typically found in New England gardens. Compared to other leguminous trees like black locust, laburnum has much more delicate three-part leaves rather than pinnately compound ones, and its flowers hang in graceful chains rather than standing upright. The golden-yellow color and drooping habit of the flower clusters make it unmistakable among flowering trees in the pea family.
